pamphlet_excerpts: Mark of Skilled Craftsmanship: Making the proper splices in the proper places on your ropes is the benchmark of a skilled craftsman (p. 11).
Premier Ropework Skill Priority: Very often, the ability to do a neat job of splicing is placed on the top of the skills list ofropework (p. 11).
Accessible Technique for Scouts: Making splices is not really all that hard (p. 11).
Three Fundamental Rope Splices: There are three basic types of splices that are typically made on three-strand twisted rope, an eye splice, a back splice, and a short splice (p. 11).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Approach Splicing with Confidence: Making splices is not really all that hard (p. 11).
Step 2 - Select the Proper Splice: There are three basic types of splices that are typically made on three-strand twisted rope, an eye splice, a back splice, and a short splice (p. 11).
Step 3 - Unlay and Weave Strands: The process in all three splices is tounlay the strands at the end of the rope, then weave them over and under back into the rope to form (p. 11).
Step 4 - Replace Bulky Rope Knots: Knots are more bulky than an eye splice or short splice (p. 11).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When tensioning a pioneering structure with a block-and-tackle or rope tackle under heavy load, why must Scouts never stand inside the bight of a rope or in the line of pull?
quiz_item.question: When tensioning a pioneering structure with a block-and-tackle or rope tackle under heavy load, why must Scouts never stand inside the bight of a rope or in the line of pull?
options: A. Standing on the rope increases friction inside the pulley sheaves and wears out natural manila fibers.
B. Body weight near the anchor stake loosens square lashings on the main A-frame spars.
C. Standing in the bight prevents the signal caller from seeing hand signals from the anchor crew.
D. If a strained rope, lashing, or anchor fails or slips, the rope can snap back violently across the bight or recoil along the line of pull, causing severe injury.
choices: A. Standing on the rope increases friction inside the pulley sheaves and wears out natural manila fibers.
B. Body weight near the anchor stake loosens square lashings on the main A-frame spars.
C. Standing in the bight prevents the signal caller from seeing hand signals from the anchor crew.
D. If a strained rope, lashing, or anchor fails or slips, the rope can snap back violently across the bight or recoil along the line of pull, causing severe injury.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. If a strained rope, lashing, or anchor fails or slips, the rope can snap back violently across the bight or recoil along the line of pull, causing severe injury.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): A rope or anchor under tension stores dangerous kinetic energy; staying clear of the bight (loop) and the direct line of pull prevents getting caught or struck if the line parts or an anchor pulls free.

Temporary Strand End Whipping: With pieces of string or some tape, temporarily whip the ends of each strand (p. 52).
Forming the Crown Knot: Make a crown knot by bending each end over its neighbor in turn, going the same way round as the lay of the rope (p. 52).
Over-and-Under Strand Tucking: Tuck each end in turn over the adjoining main strand and under the next (p. 52).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Tie Initial Crown Knot: Make a crown knot by bending each end over its neighbor in turn, going the same way round as the lay of the rope (p. 52).
Step 2 - Tuck Strands: Tuck each end in turn over the adjoining main strand and under the next (p. 52).
Step 3 - Complete Three Full Tucks: Continue over and under one in turn at least three times (p. 52).
Step 4 - Join Ropes Without Knots: A short splice can be used in place of a knot to join two ropes or the ends of the same rope together (p. 52).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Repeat Tight Half Knots: Keep repeating the half knots, front and back, pulling each one tight, until the whipping has been formed (p. 13).

pamphlet_excerpts: Simple Strop Lashing Method: A strop lashing is easy to tie (p. 10).
Midpoint Wraps and Knot: Halve the rope, place the midpoint behind what you'relashing, wrap both ends around the spars a few times and finish with asquare knot (p. 10).
Four Identical A-Frame Subassemblies: Build four identical A-frames using the 8-foot spars for the two legs and 6-foot spars for the ledger (p. 10).
Matching Ledger Height Alignment: Make sure the ledgers of each A-frame cross the legs at the same height and that the tips of the legs intersect at an equal distance from the tops (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Assemble Four Matching A-Frames: Build four identical A-frames using the 8-foot spars for the two legs and 6-foot spars for the ledger (p. 10).
Step 2 - Align Ledgers and Tips: Make sure the ledgers of each A-frame cross the legs at the same height and that the tips of the legs intersect at an equal distance from the tops (p. 10).
Step 3 - Tie Three Square Lashings: Lash each A-frame together with three tight square lashings (p. 10).
Step 4 - Join Paired A-Frame Sections: When you have four identical A-frames, lash two of them together (p. 10).

D. With West Country whippings wrapped around all three intersections
choices: A. With three tight square lashings at identical heights and tip intersections

quiz_item.correct_answer: A. With three tight square lashings at identical heights and tip intersections

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When tensioning a pioneering structure with a block-and-tackle or rope tackle under heavy load, why must Scouts never stand inside the bight of a rope or in the line of pull?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When tensioning a pioneering structure with a block-and-tackle or rope tackle under heavy load, why must Scouts never stand inside the bight of a rope or in the line of pull?
options: A. Standing on the rope increases friction inside the pulley sheaves and wears out natural manila fibers.
B. Body weight near the anchor stake loosens square lashings on the main A-frame spars.
C. Standing in the bight prevents the signal caller from seeing hand signals from the anchor crew.
D. If a strained rope, lashing, or anchor fails or slips, the rope can snap back violently across the bight or recoil along the line of pull, causing severe injury.
choices: A. Standing on the rope increases friction inside the pulley sheaves and wears out natural manila fibers.
B. Body weight near the anchor stake loosens square lashings on the main A-frame spars.
C. Standing in the bight prevents the signal caller from seeing hand signals from the anchor crew.
D. If a strained rope, lashing, or anchor fails or slips, the rope can snap back violently across the bight or recoil along the line of pull, causing severe injury.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. If a strained rope, lashing, or anchor fails or slips, the rope can snap back violently across the bight or recoil along the line of pull, causing severe injury.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): A rope or anchor under tension stores dangerous kinetic energy; staying clear of the bight (loop) and the direct line of pull prevents getting caught or struck if the line parts or an anchor pulls free.

B. Form one overhand loop followed by one underhand loop and interlock them
C. Twist a single figure-eight loop in the bight and fold both ends backward
D. Form two left overhand loops and slide the first loop on top of the second

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When forming a back splice on a three-strand twisted rope, what is the minimum number of times each strand should be tucked over and under after tying the crown knot?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When forming a back splice on a three-strand twisted rope, what is the minimum number of times each strand should be tucked over and under after tying the crown knot?
options: A. At least three times in turn
B. Exactly once before trimming flush
C. Two times in the same direction as the lay
D. Seven times with half-hitch locking wraps
choices: A. At least three times in turn
B. Exactly once before trimming flush

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. At least three times in turn
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): After forming the crown knot, you tuck each end in turn over the adjoining main strand and under the next, continuing at least three times (p. 52).

B. As long as the diameter of the rope, finished with a square knot
C. At least three inches long regardless of rope size, finished with a sheet bend
D. Half the diameter of the rope, secured by melting the natural fibers
choices: A. Twice the circumference of the rope, secured with a clove hitch
